title: Long-term observation of the endothelium morphology and corneal thickness in myopic adolescents treated with orthokeratology: a 10-year retrospective study
authors: Li-Qiong Zhao; Ying Li; Bi-Ying Wang; Bei Du; Jane Beeman; Rui-Hua Wei; Lin Liu
abstract:
AIM: To assess the long-term safety of orthokeratology (ortho-k) in myopic children by evaluating changes in corneal endothelial morphology and central corneal thickness (CCT) after prolonged ortho-k lens wear.
METHODS: This study included 65 myopic children (130 eyes). The ortho-k group comprised 39 children who had worn ortho-k lenses for more than 10y. The control group included 26 children who wore single-vision spectacles for myopia correction. Clinical data and adverse events were documented throughout the follow-up period. Endothelial cell density (ECD), coefficient of variation (CV) of cell area, percentage of hexagonal cells (%SIX), and CCT were measured at baseline and at the final follow-up visit.
RESULTS: The 39 participants (18 males, 21 females) enrolled in the ortho-k group completed the 10-year follow-up examinations successfully. The ages ranged from 7 to 12 (9.24±1.26)y. In the control group, 26 participants (13 males, 13 females) were successfully recalled and completed their 10th year examinations. The ages ranged from 7 to 12 (9.62±1.68)y. In the ortho-k group, ECD was 3119.86±202.07 cells/mm² at baseline and 3057.42±264.52 cells/mm² at the 10-year follow-up (P=0.058). CV was 30.78%±6.70% and 32.45%±7.87% (P=0.053). %SIX was 62.23%±13.07% and 60.31%±11.59% (P=0.234). CCT decreased by 8±4 μm at the 6-month visit and remained stable thereafter (538.85±43.61 μm at 6mo vs 540.78±41.44 μm at 10y, P=0.528). At the 10-year follow-up, no significant between-group differences were observed in ECD, CV, %SIX, or CCT (all P&#x003E;0.05).
CONCLUSION: This 10-year retrospective study demonstrates that long-term ortho-k lens wear has no significant adverse effects on corneal endothelial morphology or CCT compared with spectacle wear. Ortho-k shows excellent long-term safety with regard to corneal endothelial parameters and CCT, comparable to that of conventional spectacle correction in myopic children.

title: Cross-sectional study of calves from Norwegian dairy herds with enzootic pneumonia: pathogen occurrence, antimicrobial resistance, culture result interpretation, and sampling site agreement
authors: Lise M. Ånestad; Silje E. Falkeid; Veslemøy S. Oma; Randi T. Garmo; Ane M. Bjelland; Amelia R. Woolums; Maria Stokstad; Thea B. Klem
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background
                    
                      Enzootic pneumonia in calves is associated with pathogens such as
                      Pasteurellaceae
                      bacteria and
                      Mycoplasmopsis bovis
                      . Some of these bacteria are commensals in healthy calves, complicating culture interpretation, discouraging laboratory diagnostic use, and limiting knowledge of their impact. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence and antimicrobial resistance pattern of respiratory pathogens in calves from dairy herds with enzootic pneumonia. Culture results between upper and lower airway sites in healthy and diseased calves were also compared to evaluate their diagnostic value. A cross-sectional study was conducted on 131 calves (72 healthy and 59 diseased) from nine Norwegian dairy herds. Nasal swabs (NS), nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS), and serum were obtained from each calf, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from 113 calves.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      At the calf level,
                      Pasteurella multocida
                      was present in 60%,
                      Mannheimia haemolytica
                      in 55%, and
                      Histophilus somni
                      in 3%. At the sampling site level, from NS, NPS, and BAL,
                      P. multocida
                      was detected in 47%, 45%, and 27%, and
                      M. haemolytica
                      in 46%, 37%, and 8%, respectively.
                      H. somni
                      was detected in ≤ 2% per site.
                      P. multocida
                      appeared as pure culture in 73% (22/30) of positive BAL cultures. Serum antibodies to
                      M. bovis
                      were not detected. Most
                      Pasteurellaceae
                      isolates were susceptible to penicillin and other common pneumonia antimicrobials (disc diffusion). The exceptions were penicillin-resistant
                      M. haemolytica
                      isolates in two calves. Logistic regression identified an association between dominant, abundant cultures of
                      P. multocida
                      from BAL and clinical disease. Agreement for
                      P. multocida
                      detection between NS and NPS cultures and BAL was fair (kappa). Positive predictive values of
                      P. multocida
                      culture results at different abundance levels in NS and NPS, relative to BAL, were at most 49%.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    
                      P. multocida
                      was the predominant bacterium in lungs of calves from Norwegian dairy herds with enzootic pneumonia, and its abundance in the lungs may help differentiate infection from colonization in clinically diseased calves.
                      M. haemolytica
                      and
                      H. somni
                      appeared to have less clinical impact. Antimicrobial resistance appeared to be low. Upper airway cultures were inaccurate predictors of bacterial presence and abundance in the lungs and must be interpreted carefully alongside other diagnostic tools.

title: Comparison of four different techniques for lenticule dissection in small incision lenticule extraction
authors: Man-Li Liu; Quan Liu; Chong-De Long
abstract:
AIM: To compare the safety, efficacy, and technical demands of four lenticule-dissection techniques-dry dissection, continuous curvilinear lenticulorrhexis (CCL), wet dissection, and Viscoat-assisted dissection-in small incision lenticule extraction (SMILE), and to identify the method that minimizes tissue damage while preserving corneal clarity and early visual quality.
METHODS: Twenty-eight eyes undergoing SMILE were assigned to four groups: dry dissection (n=10), CCL (n=5), wet dissection (n=10), and Viscoat-assisted dissection (n=3). Surgical interfaces were evaluated with in vivo confocal microscopy and the anterior and posterior lenticule surfaces were examined by scanning electron microscopy. Two masked observers scored surface quality using four predefined criteria (surface relief, regularity of surface structure, proportion of irregular surface, and location of irregular area). Intraoperative dissection time, operator-reported technical difficulty, and early postoperative corneal clarity/interface reaction were recorded.
RESULTS: Mean anterior surface scores were: dry 10.87±1.28; CCL 13.60±0.51; wet 13.67±0.48; Viscoat 4.22±0.44. Mean posterior surface scores were: dry 10.87±1.53; CCL 13.60±0.63; wet 14.10±0.48; Viscoat 4.33±0.50. Lenticules obtained via CCL and wet dissection showed significantly better surface quality than those from dry dissection and Viscoat-assisted dissection (all P&#x003C;0.01). Wet dissection produced surface quality comparable to CCL while being technically easier to perform; dissection times were similar between dry (48.8±3.58s) and wet (48.4±1.71s) techniques (P=0.123). Viscoat-assisted cases demonstrated transient early postoperative corneal opacity that resolved as the viscoelastic was absorbed in 2wk; no significant early interface residue or lasting opacity was observed after wet dissection.
CONCLUSION: Wet dissection achieves lenticule surface quality comparable to CCL but with lower technical difficulty and without significant early postoperative adverse effects, making it a safe, effective, and easily adoptable option for lenticule separation in SMILE. Lenticule surface-quality scoring provides a practical surrogate for assessing tissue damage across dissection methods.

title: PDO ML/AI Success Story: Optimizing ESP Wells with Predictive Failure Detection
authors: Salim Al Harthi; Issa Balushi; Aziz Bimani; Mansi Jani; Nitish Kumar; Anand Raosaheb More
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Objectives/Scope
                    The project introduced an advanced early failure prediction system for Electrical Submersible Pump (ESP) wells through a collaborative effort. This initiative was carried out in phases—starting with development, followed by operationalization and a value-driven assessment. It focused on two PDO assets, covering over 400 active ESP wells. By embedding predictive insights into daily operations, the system aimed to enhance decision-making, reduce unplanned downtime, and optimize overall well performance.
                  
                  
                    Methods, Procedures, Process
                    The Well Management System (WMS) integrated real-time data, physics-based inputs, and machine learning (ML) models to calculate failure probability scores and generate daily alarms. Outputs were analyzed through trend reports and field actions, facilitating ongoing preventive maintenance. The project team worked with ESP engineers to interpret the insights and plan proactive interventions. By optimizing operational parameters and troubleshooting effectively, the system helped to prevent ESP failures, increase run life, restore stable well performance, and minimize production disruptions, enhancing overall efficiency and cost savings.
                  
                  
                    Results, Observations, Conclusions
                    Over a four-month period, the project team utilized failure prediction insights to mitigate operational challenges and save multiple ESP wells from failure. The predictive model demonstrated a 67% success rate in forecasting failures ahead of time and achieved 87% precision in alarm accuracy, correctly identifying failed ESP wells and enabling timely corrective actions, such as elective pulls. With a model accuracy of 97%, failure-prone conditions were identified an average of 58 days in advance, allowing engineers to take corrective actions and avoid operational disruptions. This proactive approach led to a 2.75% reduction in ESP failure rates, extending the run life of the wells and preventing potential oil deferment. Financially, the project resulted in savings of 3.6 million USD, reducing the need for costly hoist interventions and preventing production deferment. By integrating predictive insights into daily operations, the team improved operational efficiency, lowered costs, and enhanced well reliability, demonstrating the tangible value of early failure prediction for ESP wells.
                  
                  
                    Novel/Additive Information
                    This paper introduces a scalable method for integrating predictive analytics into live production environments. It highlights the importance of data-driven decision-making and seamless integration of machine learning insights into operational workflows. The model's cognitive adaptation into daily actions has proven valuable in generating tangible results, such as improved well performance and cost savings. Furthermore, the approach sets the stage for future prescriptive models that can optimize ESP operations by combining predictive and actionable insights.

title: Improving Fracture Detection in High-Resistivity Steam-Injection Wells Using High-Resolution Ultrasonic LWD Imaging Sensors
authors: Ahmed Taher; Samya Al Sawafi; Salim Al Shuaili; Maitham Al Humaid
abstract:
Abstract
                  Carbonate reservoirs are characterized by complex geological structures and unpredictable fracture networks, which significantly influence fluid flow and reservoir performance. Water-injection wells are commonly drilled to enhance sweeping efficiency, and their injectivity is largely governed by effective permeability and the presence of natural fractures. Accurate evaluation of these fractures is critical for understanding and optimizing injectivity.
                  Steam-injection wells drilled in high-resistivity formations present challenges for LWD micro-resistivity imaging tools, used for near-wellbore fracture characterization. Poor image contrast and reduced sensitivity to resistive features impair the ability to identify natural fractures, drilling-induced fractures, vugs, and breakout geometries. This study presents the deployment of high-resolution ultrasonic LWD imaging sensors as an effective alternative for fracture detection in high-resistivity steam-injection environments in North Oman. Field results demonstrate superior image clarity, improved structural interpretation, and enhanced operational decision-making.
                  The micro-resistivity imaging tool provides high-resolution electrical images designed for identifying bedding, fractures, and sedimentary features in conductive mud systems. The ultrasonic imaging tool, which generates amplitude and travel-time maps from acoustic reflections, performs reliably in both conductive and non-conductive muds. While micro-resistivity imaging offers fine-scale geological resolution in conductive mud systems, ultrasonic imaging provides continuous borehole geometry measurements and fracture and structural mapping in high-resistivity formations. Bottomhole assemblies were utilized without a driver system, to drill short, horizontal sections for steam injection and enabling measurements closer to the bit. The sections were logged with gamma ray, resistivity, high-resolution micro-resistivity, and ultrasonic imaging tools. The collar incorporating gamma ray, directional, and ultrasonic imaging sensors was placed directly above the bit.
                  Field deployments of the ultrasonic imaging tool across multiple steam-injection wells in North Oman demonstrated significant improvements in image quality compared to micro-resistivity imaging. Ultrasonic images revealed fracture networks previously undetectable with micro-resistivity tools, improving understanding of fracture orientation, density, and connectivity.
                  Ultrasonic imaging covered more of the horizontal section, as it was closer to the bit than the micro-resistivity tool, which was placed almost 20 m away from the bit. The ultrasonic images provided better resolution of all conductive features picked along the section, while the micro-resistivity images lost sensitivity in very high-resistivity intervals, degrading their ability to detect some of the finer features.
                  The results confirm that ultrasonic imaging can overcome some of the inherent limitations of micro-resistivity tools, offering a robust solution for fracture characterization and injectivity optimization in steam-driven EOR developments. The study concludes that adopting LWD high-resolution ultrasonic imaging in steam-injection wells with high-resistivity formations delivers a practical balance between operational efficiency and imaging adequacy. The resulting improvements in drilling speed and data continuity contribute to reduced nonproductive time and optimized well-delivery performance.

title: Fluorescein spectrofluorometric quenching detection of chloride and iodide using eight-Blue-LEDs excitation and dual solar cells
authors: Ghufran K. Allawi; N. S. Turkey
abstract:
Abstract
                  This study presents a novel, custom‑built fluorescence detector for the precise determination of chloride and iodide ions based on their quenching effect on fluorescein. The detection system incorporates eight blue LEDs irradiation sources arranged at 0–90° angles relative to twin solar cell detectors connected. Two fluorescence quenching strategies were developed. The injected‑mixture mode (IMFQ) exhibited linear ranges of 0.00–1.00 mM for Cl⁻ and 0.00–1.25 mM for I⁻, with detection limits of 20 µM and 10 µmol L⁻¹, respectively. The continuous‑flow mode (CFFQ) demonstrated superior sensitivity with a dispersion factor of 1.33, wider linear ranges (0.1–6.0 mM for Cl⁻ and 0.05–6.0 mM for I⁻), and lower detection limits (10 µM and 5 µM, respectively). Both strategies rely on Stern‑Volmer kinetics and were successfully applied to real samples (table salts and detergents) with excellent recoveries (95.7–108.1%).

title: Short versus long myotomy during peroral endoscopic myotomy for achalasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Zain Ul Abideen; Muhammad Hassan Waseem; Rimmel Ali; Avan Chu; Muhammad Sheraz Hameed; Abdullah; Noor-Ul-Huda Ramzan; Pawan Kumar Thada; Prasun Kumar Jalal
abstract:
Background:
                    Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is an established treatment modality for achalasia. This meta-analysis aimed to compare the clinically relevant outcomes of short and long myotomy during POEM for achalasia.
                  
                  
                    Methods:
                    PubMed, Cochrane Central, and ScienceDirect were systematically searched from inception to February 2025. The risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) were pooled using the random-effects model in Review Manager. Quality assessment was conducted using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 2.0) tool and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
                  
                  
                    Results:
                    
                      Seven studies, pooling a total of 737 patients, were included in the analysis. The short myotomy showed no significant difference in clinical success [RR: 1.02; 95% CI: (0.99–1.05);
                      P
                      = 0.19], Eckardt score (
                      P
                      = 0.45), or lower esophageal sphincter pressure (
                      P
                      = 0.72) compared to the long myotomy. Similarly, the integrated relaxation pressures (
                      P
                      = 0.73), duration of hospitalization (
                      P
                      = 0.67), and the risk of erosive esophagitis (
                      P
                      = 0.13) were comparable between the two arms. The short myotomy arm significantly reduced overall procedural duration [MD: −15.84; 95% CI: (−21.05 to −10.63);
                      P
                      < 0.00001]. Short myotomy was also associated with a significantly lower risk of abnormal esophageal acid exposure [RR: 0.64; 95% CI: (0.43–0.95);
                      P
                      = 0.03].
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion:
                    Short myotomy was associated with a significant reduction in procedural time and risk of abnormal esophageal acid exposure, whereas the remaining efficacy and safety endpoints were comparable between the two techniques.

title: Digital Twin-Based Detection of Water Coning in Multilateral Wells: A Smart Approach for Sustaining Performance
authors: Rawan Alodily; Mohammad Al-Kadem
abstract:
Abstract
                  Water coning remains a critical challenge in the operation of multilateral wells, often leading to premature water breakthrough, rapid decline in oil rate, and increased production costs. This study seeks to answer the question: How can digital twin well modeling be used to identify and detect early water coning in multilateral wells? The objective is to establish a robust workflow for coning detection using real-time simulation and sensitivity analysis, highlighting its direct impact on well performance, including production sustainability, inflow balancing, and delaying excessive water cut.
                  A hybrid methodology was employed, combining physics-based well modeling in Schlumberger PIPESIM with digital twin integration for live data calibration. Each lateral was represented as an independent well, assembled into a network to mimic multilateral well geometry. Analytical IPR models were applied to define reservoir inflow, with sensitivity studies conducted on drawdown, choke settings, permeability, and skin. Water cut and WOR responses were analyzed per lateral to identify deviations signaling water coning onset. Real-time allocation and calibration against measured flow and pressure data ensured that the digital twin maintained fidelity. Diagnostic indicators such as WOR acceleration, dWOR/dq, and BHP stiffening were systematically evaluated.
                  The analysis demonstrated that water coning can be identified at early stages by monitoring disproportionate increases in WOR for small rate increments, particularly in heel-dominated laterals. PIPESIM-based sensitivity sweeps revealed that laterals closer to the water contact showed sharp WC upturns at lower drawdowns compared to toe laterals, providing a reliable diagnostic pattern. A controlled choke reduction on the affected lateral consistently lowered WC while maintaining stable oil production from the others, confirming the presence of coning. Furthermore, water cut imbalance across laterals proved to be an early indicator of localized breakthrough. The digital twin's predictive capabilities allowed proactive operational decisions such as rate redistribution and lateral-specific choke management, which resulted in sustaining oil output while minimizing water handling. These observations confirm that digital twin well modeling provides both a detection framework and a decision-support tool for mitigating the negative impact of water coning on well performance.
                  This study introduces a structured digital twin workflow for multilateral wells that can differentiate water coning from channeling or completion integrity issues. Unlike conventional monitoring, which often relies on surface WC alarms after the problem has escalated, this approach provides lateral-specific early detection and actionable mitigation strategies. The novelty lies in linking PIPESIM sensitivity analysis with live twin calibration to deliver real-time, branch-level coning diagnostics a step change toward intelligent well management.

title: Comparison of neurohormone and callus volume formation in long bone fractures associated with or without traumatic brain injury
authors: Prabu Mounisamy; Hrushikesh Singh; Balasubramaniyan Vairappan; Gopikrishnan Rajasekar; Sushma Chandrashekar; Naveen Jeyaraman; Madhan Jeyaraman
abstract:
BACKGROUND
                  Fracture healing is a dynamic process influenced by systemic and local factors. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) has been clinically associated with accelerated bone repair, yet the underlying biochemical mechanisms remain unclear.
                  AIM
                  To investigate the roles of growth hormone (GH), parathyroid hormone (PTH), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) in callus formation among patients with long bone fractures, comparing cohorts with and without TBI.
                  METHODS
                  A prospective analytical study was conducted at JIPMER from January 2023 to December 2025. Patients with diaphyseal long bone fractures were stratified into two groups: With TBI and without TBI. Serum levels of GH, PTH, and IL-6 were measured at defined intervals using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Callus volume was assessed radiologically via  computed tomography imaging at 4 weeks and 6 weeks post-injury. Statistical analysis included RMANOVA and correlation studies to evaluate biomarker trends and their association with callus formation.
                  RESULTS
                  Patients with concomitant TBI exhibited significantly elevated levels of GH and PTH during early healing phases, while IL-6 levels showed a complex temporal pattern. Callus volume was markedly higher in the TBI group at both 4 weeks and 6 weeks, with statistically significant differences (P  < 0.05). Positive correlations were observed between GH/PTH levels and callus volume, whereas IL-6 showed inverse associations in certain phases.
                  CONCLUSION
                  TBI appears to modulate systemic hormonal and cytokine responses that favor enhanced osteogenesis. Elevated GH and PTH levels may contribute to accelerated callus formation, while IL-6’s role remains context-dependent. These findings offer potential therapeutic insights for improving fracture healing outcomes.

title: AI Driven Detection of Early Leakage Pathways Using Time Lapse Pressure, Temperature, Flow, and Geochemical (CO2 Concentration) Signals in Subsurface CCUS Systems
authors: P. Saini; U. Biradar; K. Sonawane; A. Mehta; D. Chauhan; P. Basu
abstract:
Abstract
                  Secure and verifiable long-term containment of CO₂ in deep subsurface formations is essential for the success of large-scale CCUS deployment. However, reservoir heterogeneity, legacy wells, micro-fractures, and fault networks create potential pathways for unintended CO₂ migration. Traditional observation practices periodic logs, infrequent pressure surveys, and sparse geochemical sampling often fail to detect early-stage leakage indicators that appear subtly within high-frequency operational signals. This study aims to develop and validate an AI-enabled diagnostic system that integrates time-lapse pressure, temperature, flow rate, and CO₂ concentration signals from injection and monitoring wells to identify emerging leakage pathways, quantify risk levels, and improve containment assurance across a range of geological storage settings.&#x2028;
                  The proposed methodology is structured around four integrated components:
                  High-resolution subsurface data acquisition using downhole pressure-temperature gauges, multi-phase flow sensors, wellhead instrumentation, and distributed Fiber-optic measurements where available. Physics-based reservoir modelling, including pressure propagation, thermal gradients, multiphase CO₂ behaviour, expected saturation fronts, and geochemical evolution under normal injection conditions to provide a dynamic baseline. Machine-learning-driven anomaly detection employing LSTM and auto-encoder architectures to identify multivariate deviations, combined with clustering algorithms that classify patterns linked to micro-annulus formation, inter-well connectivity, fault activation, or cement degradation. Probabilistic leakage pathway classification, translating anomaly signatures into actionable risk indicators and spatial diagnostics for engineers and regulators. The system continuously compares real-time sensor data against synthetic physics outputs to calculate drift scores and generate a dynamic leakage likelihood index.
                  Evaluation using historical datasets and synthetic reservoir scenarios shows that the AI system can detect potential leakage-related anomalies 7-14 days earlier than conventional monitoring. The multivariate learning models improved sensitivity to micro-leakage signals by 25 to 40% compared to static thresholds. Pressure-temperature correlation analysis revealed thermodynamic deviations associated with slow CO₂ migration, while flow-imbalance patterns identified mass discrepancies corresponding to early breakthrough or crossflow. Concentration signals enhanced detection of subtle plume divergence and unexpected geochemical mixing. Across heterogenous reservoirs, depleted fields, and deep saline aquifers, the hybrid physics AI approach remained stable under varying injection rates and operational noise. Overall, the diagnostic workflow supports earlier decision-making, improved containment assurance, and reduced remediation costs.
                  This work introduces a first of its kind hybrid physics AI diagnostic engine that simultaneously analyses pressure, temperature, flow, and CO₂ concentration signals to detect early leakage pathways in subsurface CO₂ storage. Unlike traditional monitoring methods, this system delivers continuous, real-time, data-driven leakage diagnostics, integrates geomechanics and geochemistry patterns, and provides automated root-cause classification. The approach transforms raw subsurface operations data into predictive intelligence, offering operators and regulators higher confidence in long-term CO₂ containment and enabling safer, more scalable CCUS deployment.

title: Curing Condensate Banking: From Alcohol Treatment to Long-Term Wettability Alteration: Application to Deep Tight Gas Wells in the Sultanate of Oman
authors: Ghusun Al Aamri; Naima Spurr; Billy Gray; Xiaolan Wang; Kimberly Lant; Ahmed Alrashdi
abstract:
Abstract
                  Condensate banking is a major issue in Sultanate of Oman, especially in tight gas reservoirs, where extraction of natural gas has led to deposition of condensate in the near-wellbore area. Production can decline very sharply. Successful field applications developed with alcohol treatments in deep tight sandstone gas wells have minimized the impact of such phenomenon on production and accelerated the post-completion flow-back operations in the Sultanate of Oman. While these methods have been greatly beneficial, in many cases the treatments require reapplication after a short period of time. An innovative technology that provides remedial treatment and modifies the wettability of the formation to a near neutral state is introduced for application in the Sultanate of Oman fields. Such surface modifier is covalently bonded to the reservoir rock, creating a robust engineered surface with low surface energy potentially leading to sustained production for extended periods of time.
                  Thorough lab testing and screening processes to determine an effective formulation were performed. In particular, the solvent package with the new active material was optimized to increase and maintain production for extended periods of time. Furthermore, compatibility studies between the new treatments and the highly saline formation water were performed. Core flow was used as the primary test protocol to determine the efficacy of this treatment for three fields in Sultanate of Oman that are suffering from condensate banking.
                  Several alcohol treatment jobs were conducted on gas wells impacted by condensate banking. While the treatments restored the gas production and condensate rate, in many case the success was for a limited time and the condensate banking re-accumulated quickly. As seen in the laboratory core flow testing, the new system has the potential of sustained production for extended periods of time. The results show that once the core is treated with this new technology, the bank cannot be re-formed, and the condensate is produced after repeated cycles. These results show longevity of the treatment. In comparison, the alcohol treatment shows a decrease in relative permeability to gas, once the condensate is rebuilt. This technology is applicable to both sandstone and carbonate reservoirs. These early promising results have resulted in planning a field trial to determine the efficacy of such treatment in fields impacted by liquid blockage impairment.
                  Using this new technology in alcohol treatments to remove condensate banking improved efficiency in both time and materials. A solution that will eliminate the banking will improve production in tight gas fields.

title: A Novel Alternative to SAGD: Enhancing Ultra-Heavy Oil Recovery with an Integrated Steam-CO2-Solvent Huff-N-Puff Process
authors: Yao Wang; Liguo Zhong; Yixin Fu; Zhou Yang; Xuhong Ouyang; Hua Long
abstract:
Abstract
                  Aiming at the technical bottlenecks of conventional SAGD in developing ultra-heavy oil in Block D84 of Liaohe Oilfield, such as severe steam override, difficulty establishing thermal communication and low oil-steam ratio, this study employed laboratory experiments, physical simulation, and numerical modeling. Laboratory experiments were conducted to test the viscosity-temperature characteristics of heavy oil, explore the synergistic viscosity and interfacial tension reduction effects of the CO2-n-hexane system, and determine its optimal ratio. Physical simulation experiments verified the enhanced development effect of the CO2-n-hexane system assisted SAGD. CMG software was used to build a reservoir numerical model, analyze the influence laws of injection timing and injection-production parameters on development effect, and optimize the field-adapted parameters. This research elucidated the synergistic mechanism of the CO2-n-hexane system, determined the optimal injection-production scheme for field application, and provides comprehensive theoretical and technical guidance for the industrial promotion of CO2-solvent assisted SAGD technology in Block D84.

title: A novel YOLO-NAS algorithm for android malware detection using histogram of oriented gradients (HOG) based feature extraction
authors: Shanmuga Priya Gopalakrishnan; Rama Subra Mani Vanamamalai
abstract: Smartphones have developed into more than just communication tools in the current digital era, becoming essential to many facets of daily life. Because of its large user base and open-source nature, Android is a dominant mobile operating system. But because of its extensive use, it has become a prominent target for more complex malware attacks. This efficient deep learning-based framework for Android virus detection uses a proposed You Only Look Once based Neural Architecture Search (YOLO-NAS) model in conjunction with feature selection techniques. The system first receives a dataset of Android malware, after which data preparation is carried out to enhance data quality, remove noise, and standardize features. A Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) model is used to identify the most pertinent and discriminative features from the processed dataset in order to decrease dimensionality and increase computing efficiency. The YOLO-NAS model, which classifies malware in a two-class environment as either benign or malicious, is then fed the enhanced feature set. The proposed YOLO-NAS concept aims to improve detection accuracy without compromising robustness or scalability. Performance is assessed using common measures such as F1-Score, Accuracy, Precision, and Recall. The suggested method is appropriate for real-time Android security applications since testing results show that YOLO-NAS and enhanced feature extraction greatly enhance malware detection capabilities.

title: Refinement Feature Fusion for Multi-model Depression Detection
authors: Yongwei Liao; Yinbin Zhang; Weiwei Chen; Zhenjun Li; Bing Zhou
abstract:
Abstract
                This paper proposes UniMDD (Unified Multi-modal Depression Detection), a novel framework designed for multimodal depression detection based on video interviews. It employs an efficient multi-model data fusion strategy, comprising four sequential modules: feature extraction, feature fusion, feature refinement, and depression detection. Specifically, the feature extraction module leverages OpenFace for facial features, VGGish for audio features, and a Large Language Model for textual features. The core innovation lies in the fusion and refinement stages. The feature fusion module designs a Mixed Attention Network(MAN) to capture intricate cross-modal interactions and effectively integrate complementary information from different data streams. Subsequently, the feature refinement module constructs an EHA-Attention mechanism within decoder blocks. This serves a dual purpose: it generates higher-level semantic and contextual representations while mitigating potential inter-modal conflicts and enhancing the comprehension of each individual modality. Finally, the refined features are fed into the depression detection module for prediction. Experimental validation on the LMVD dataset demonstrates that UniMDD achieves an accuracy of 76.68%, surpassing the current state-of-the-art method, DepMamba, by a margin of 4.55 percentage points. These results underscore the advancement and robustness of the proposed UniMDD framework.

title: Evaluation of serum progranulin as a biomarker for early detection of neonatal sepsis in a microbiological context
authors: Sherien F. Belasy; Abdullah M. Abdo; Sohaila A. Abdel-Halim; Noha N. M. Salah-Eldeen; Safaa M. Abdel-Rahman; Amal M. Soliman
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Background
                    
                      Neonatal sepsis remains a major contributor to neonatal morbidity and mortality worldwide. The nonspecific nature of clinical signs and the limited sensitivity of conventional microbiological methods, such as blood culture, often hinder early diagnosis. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of serum progranulin (PGRN) in comparison with established biomarkers—procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP)—in the early detection of suspected neonatal sepsis before microbiological confirmation, thereby supporting prompt clinical decision-making. Methods: A total of 60 neonates with clinically suspected sepsis and 30 healthy controls were enrolled. Before initiation of antimicrobial therapy, blood samples were collected for microbiological culture, complete blood count, and platelet count. Additional samples were analyzed for CRP, PCT, and PGRN levels using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Diagnostic accuracy was determined using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results: Serum PGRN levels were significantly elevated in the sepsis group compared to controls (77.26 vs. 28.78 ng/mL; Mann–Whitney
                      p
                       < 0.001). PGRN demonstrated excellent diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.986; 95% CI 0.957–1.000;
                      p
                       < 0.001), outperforming both PCT (AUC = 0.772; 95% CI 0.666–0.877;
                      p
                       < 0.001) and CRP (AUC = 0.833; 95% CI 0.752–0.915;
                      p
                       < 0.001). At a cut-off of 35.80 ng/mL, PGRN yielded a sensitivity of 98.31% and a negative predictive value of 96.7%. Combined assessment of PGRN and PCT further enhanced diagnostic sensitivity and specificity. Conclusion: Serum progranulin is a promising biomarker for the early diagnosis of neonatal sepsis and demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy compared to PCT and CRP. When integrated with conventional microbiological testing and PCT measurement, PGRN can substantially improve early detection rates, enable timely therapeutic intervention, and potentially reduce sepsis-related mortality in neonates.

title: Increasing Operational Efficiency in Micro-Fracking Decisions Through Automated Breakout Detection from Ultrasonic Borehole Images: A Machine Learning-Based Approach
authors: L. B. Elkaissi; I. Stepanov; R. Goswami; M. Nassar
abstract:
Summary
                  
                    Objectives/Scope
                    Accurate estimation of in-situ stress orientation is a critical requirement for the effective design and execution of micro-fracturing operations. Borehole breakouts, which develop as stress-induced compressive failures of the borehole wall, are widely recognized as reliable indicators of the horizontal stress direction. Ultrasonic borehole imaging tools provide high-resolution measurements that enable the identification of these features. However, conventional breakout interpretation from ultrasonic images is typically performed manually, making the process time-consuming and challenging to scale across large datasets and multiple wells. These limitations hinder efficient application of breakout analysis within operational workflows.
                    This study presents a machine learning–based workflow for automated breakout detection and azimuth estimation from ultrasonic borehole images. The proposed approach aims to improve operational efficiency and ensure repeatable and consistent breakout interpretation while preserving geological and geomechanical relevance. By automating breakout identification and orientation analysis, the workflow provides a practical and reliable input for stress characterization and micro-fracturing decision-making.
                  
                  
                    Methods, Procedures, Process
                    The proposed workflow operates on unwrapped ultrasonic borehole images and integrates systematic image preparation, pixel-level feature extraction, supervised machine learning classification, and post-processing geometric analysis. Each ultrasonic image is segmented into fixed-depth slices to enable localized breakout detection while preserving depth-dependent variation. Pixel-level features are extracted directly from the ultrasonic amplitude data and their spatial relationships, providing a numerical representation of breakout-related image patterns. A supervised machine learning classifier is trained using manually annotated image slices following a human-in-the-loop strategy, allowing expert knowledge to be incorporated into the training process while maintaining control over label quality. The classifier outputs pixel-level probability maps, which are converted into binary predictions using a calibrated decision threshold. Detected regions are further refined using morphological and geometric constraints to remove noise and isolate coherent breakout features. These regions are converted into bounding boxes, from which breakout azimuths and corresponding depth intervals are computed using circular statistical methods.
                    The automated workflow demonstrates robust and repeatable detection of borehole breakouts across multiple wells and depth intervals. The resulting breakout azimuths exhibit stable orientation trends with depth and show strong agreement with manually interpreted results. Compared to conventional manual interpretation, the proposed approach significantly reduces analysis time while preserving geological interpretability and operational relevance. These results indicate that automated breakout detection can serve as a reliable and efficient input for stress orientation assessment and micro-fracturing design optimization.

title: Challenges in 1SSF Detection in 4H-SiC Epilayer and Related Failure
authors: Cristiano Calabretta; Cettina Bottari; Salvatore Adamo; Beatrice Carbone; Giovanni Maira; Fabiana Vento; Enzo Fontana; Nicolo Piluso; Mario S. Alessandrino; Alfio Russo; Patrick Fiorenza; Fabrizio Roccaforte; Andrea Severino
abstract: Basal plane dislocations (BPDs) represent one of the most detrimental defects in 4H-SiC epitaxial wafers, causing forward voltage degradation in bipolar and power FET devices through the formation and expansion of Shockley-type stacking faults (SSFs). This expansion is driven by the recombination-enhanced dislocation glide (REDG) mechanism during forward bias operation. Despite efforts to mitigate BPD effects by converting them into threading edge dislocations (TEDs) via buffer layer engineering, throughout the epitaxial growth SSFs can still nucleate and propagate, particularly under high current injection. This work presents a comprehensive analysis combining electrical characterization, fault localization technique, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and micro-photoluminescence (μ-PL) to investigate SSF formation, crystallographic features, and their impact on device performance. The results underscore the critical role of advanced diagnostics and epitaxial process optimization in controlling SSF-related degradation and improving the reliability of SiC power devices.

title: Breaking the Diagnostic Barrier: First Worldwide Application of High-Frequency Pressure Monitoring for Large Volume Acid Stimulation Evaluation in Long Open-Hole Carbonate Wells, Block-5 North Oman
authors: H. A. Mufargi; T. K. Ahmed; A. B. Pramadana; H. A. Harthi; A. M. Al Naabi; M. Al Shuelly; K. Al Busaidi; H. Al Dafai; K. Al Wahaibi; AbdulAziz Al Rawahi; Mohammed Al Abri; Mazin Al Farsi; Samir Al Sulaimi; Azza Al Mandhari; Ibrahim Al Mahrouqi; Stevanus Kurniadi; Emanuel Ibarrolaza; Hao Li
abstract:
Abstract
                  Understanding stimulation coverage and diversion efficiency in long open-hole carbonate wells has remained one of the most difficult challenges in acid stimulation. Traditional evaluation methods rely on post-job production or PLT data, providing indirect insights. It introduces the first worldwide application of High-Frequency Pressure Monitoring, a near real-time, surface-based diagnostic technology that transforms how operators evaluate acid stimulation effectiveness, zonal fluid placement and diversion performance. The objective is to establish a robust, field-proven methodology that delivers instant visibility of stimulation behavior without intrusive downhole tools or operational interruption.
                  HFPM continuously records high-resolution surface pressure data during both pumping and shut-in phases to capture subtle pressure signals that reveal downhole flow behavior. It analyzes two main types of diagnostic responses. The first, water-hammer reflections occur naturally when the pumps are shut down and provide depth-specific information about fluid entry. The second, known as heartbeat response, is intentionally created by applying controlled pump-rate pulsations during injection. These rhythmic pulses travel as pressure waves through the wellbore and reflect from active flow, allowing continuous tracking of stimulation, even in wells where water-hammer signals are weak or absent. A proprietary signal-processing algorithm then interprets these reflections using advanced time-domain and cepstrum analysis to estimate both depth and zones of stimulation. Fully surface based, HFPM system operates with single pressure sensor and compact processor box, integrating seamlessly with existing pumping operations and requiring no additional rig-up or HSE exposure
                  Field implementation in Block-5, north of Oman, demonstrated that HFPM could accurately identify fluid entry and assess the performance of various diverter systems. Treatments using foam-based diversion demonstrated effective near-wellbore isolation and represented one of the most efficient and operationally flexible diversion solutions. However, when combined with degradable solid diverters, provided slightly more stable zonal isolation and broader stimulation coverage. In one well, HFPM also detected fluid communication extending behind the liner, observation later confirmed by post-job PLT, highlighting the technology's diagnostic precision. HFPM interpretation matched PLT results within ±10%, confirming its diagnostic accuracy and reliability as surface evaluation tool. The heartbeat analysis proved valuable in wells with depleted or highly permeable zones, where traditional water-hammer signals are weak, providing reliable interpretation under challenging reservoir.
                  This pioneering deployment represents a step change in acid stimulation diagnostics, integrating water-hammer and heartbeat analyses within a single HFPM framework. The technology bridges the long-standing gap between surface pressure monitoring and downhole processes, delivering a real-time, data-driven workflow that enables engineers to optimize stimulation design on the fly, enhance diversion and maximize acid efficiency. Result is scalable, low-cost diagnostic solution to carbonate reservoirs worldwide, transforming how operators evaluate and execute large-volume acid stimulation and positioning Oman as pioneer in real-time stimulation diagnostics.

title: Production Strategy Optimization in Deep Jurassic Carbonate Reservoirs via Integrated NMR–Dielectric Logging: A Case Study from West Kuwait
authors: Mahmoud Fawzy; Elhadi Abusin; Rasha Al-Morakhi; Nguy Kim Long; Abdullah Al-Azmi; Mahmoud Kalawina; Nacer Guergueb; Zakaria Swidan; Ehab Negm
abstract:
Abstract
                  This paper presents a case study from a deep Jurassic carbonate reservoir in West Kuwait where conventional porosity–resistivity interpretation could not reliably separate producible from non-producible intervals. An integrated Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and dielectric logging workflow was applied to (1) differentiate movable hydrocarbons from irreducible or immobile fluids, (2) reduce ambiguity in water saturation in low-resistivity and heterogeneous carbonate rocks, and (3) translate the petrophysical interpretation into a selective cased-hole perforation and isolation strategy. NMR provided pore-size distribution, total and effective porosity, permeability indicators, and fluid characterization (movable oil versus irreducible/immobile oil), while the dielectric measurement delivered water-filled porosity and water saturation largely independent of formation-water salinity and common carbonate textural effects. The integrated interpretation was cross-checked with downhole pressure data and validated against available core observations. The workflow identified intervals that would have been interpreted as hydrocarbon-bearing pay by conventional logs but were shown to be dominated by immobile or heavy hydrocarbon components with limited movable fraction, posing production risk. A targeted perforation and isolation plan was then used to avoid water-bearing and non-producible zones and focus on intervals exhibiting a movable hydrocarbon component, improving confidence in completion decisions.

title: New Microbial EOR: Unlocking the Next Wave of Oil Recovery in PDO Fields
authors: A. Almahrouqi; N. M. Al Hinai
abstract:
Abstract
                  This paper presents the development and qualification of a microbial-based Organic Oil Recovery (OOR) concept as a low-cost and environmentally aligned enhanced oil recovery (EOR) solution targeting mature waterflooded reservoirs approaching the tertiary recovery stage. The objective of the study is to evaluate the technical feasibility, operational applicability, and scalability of microbial stimulation to mobilize residual oil and sustain production in late-life assets.
                  A structured, stage-gated methodology was adopted, progressing from laboratory validation to pilot design and field deployment readiness. Laboratory evaluations conducted under representative reservoir conditions confirmed microbial compatibility with selected reservoir fluids and demonstrated improved oil displacement behavior relative to baseline waterflood performance. Following laboratory qualification, reservoir screening and integrated technical review identified B-XX and Z-XX injection patterns as suitable pilot candidates based on flood maturity, high water cut, stable injectivity, and well-established injector–producer connectivity. A controlled pilot execution framework was developed utilizing existing injection infrastructure, supported by predefined success criteria, surveillance requirements, and decision gates to objectively evaluate performance.
                  While field implementation is planned for early 2026, the results to date establish technical readiness and provide confidence in the applicability of microbial-based recovery under mature reservoir conditions. The study concludes that OOR represents a scalable and operationally simple recovery pathway capable of delivering incremental production at competitive cost. The novelty of this work lies in integrating laboratory validation, reservoir screening, and structured pilot governance into a transferable framework for de-risking microbial EOR deployment prior to wider deployment.

title: Single-cell RNA sequencing unveils macrophage heterogeneity and cell-cell interactions in hepatocellular carcinoma progression
authors: YiFei Tang; JiaHui Li; LingYing Huang
abstract:
Background
                    Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents a major global health burden, characterized by complex metabolic reprogramming and immunological dysregulation. This study aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying HCC progression using integrative multi-omics analyses, with a specific focus on macrophage heterogeneity and intercellular communication networks in the tumor microenvironment.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We performed comprehensive bioinformatic analyses integrating gene expression profiling, DNA methylation data, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets from publicly available databases. Single-cell transcriptomic data (GSE149614) were processed using Seurat for quality control, dimensionality reduction, and cell type annotation. Macrophage subpopulation diversity was assessed through Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) and differential expression analysis. Intercellular communication networks were reconstructed using CellPhoneDB and CellChat to identify Signaling axes that act as primary mediators of macrophage–hepatocyte/fibroblast crosstalk in HCC. Functional enrichment analyses were conducted via Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analyses. The diagnostic and prognostic potential of genes whose expression or methylation status predicts HCC stage, metastasis risk, and patient survival was evaluated through Receiver Operating Characteristic curve analysis and survival modeling. Expression patterns of genes whose dysregulation directly disrupts immunometabolic crosstalk between macrophages and tumor cells, whose dysregulation increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma progression by promoting an immunosuppressive microenvironment and enhancing tumor cell proliferation and invasion were experimentally validated using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) in two hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines (HepG2 and Huh7) obtained from American Type Culture Collection.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    
                      Single-cell analysis revealed profound cellular heterogeneity within the HCC microenvironment, identifying six transcriptionally distinct macrophage subpopulations (M1–M6) with unique immunometabolic signatures. M2-like subsets were enriched in extracellular matrix organization and integrin-mediated signaling pathways, supporting their pro-fibrotic and immunosuppressive roles. Intercellular communication network analysis identified the SPP1–CD44/ITGAV signaling axis as a dominant pathway mediating macrophage–hepatocyte and macrophage–fibroblast interactions. APOA2 demonstrated differential expression between normal and tumor tissues, with its downregulation strongly correlated with promoter methylation (Spearman ρ = −0.31, P = 9.11 × 10
                      −10
                      ). Although APOA2 showed limited diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.552), APOA2-low tumors exhibited trends toward poorer clinical outcomes across multiple survival metrics. Integration of metabolomic and transcriptomic data revealed associations between APOA2 silencing, altered serum metabolite profiles, and enhanced macrophage activation, establishing a metabolic–immune–epigenetic cascade that promotes tumor fibrogenesis and progression. qRT-PCR validation in HCC cell lines confirmed differential expression of Genes encoding core components of the SPP1–CD44/ITGAV signaling axis that regulate macrophage–tumor crosstalk and whose expression levels correlate with higher histological grade and increased metastatic risk in hepatocellular carcinoma in aggressive Huh7 cells (3.2-fold and 2.8-fold respectively, P &lt; 0.001), while APOA2 was downregulated (0.35-fold, P &lt; 0.001), corroborating bioinformatic predictions.
                    
                  
                  
                    Conclusion
                    This study unveils Macrophages that orchestrate the majority of intercellular signaling interactions in the HCC microenvironment orchestrating the immunometabolic landscape of HCC through the SPP1–integrin signaling network. The identification of functionally distinct macrophage subpopulations and the metabolic–immune–epigenetic axis involving APOA2 provides novel mechanistic insights into HCC pathogenesis and identifies genes and signaling axes whose pharmacological inhibition can reverse immunosuppression and block HCC progression for precision intervention strategies.
